claims.text: High-Cr steels form a continuous, nanocrystalline chromium-rich oxide layer in situ under oxidizing conditions.
Chromium segregation at grain boundaries stabilizes the chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
The chromium-rich passive film inhibits ingress of corrosive species.
During oxidizing exposure, chromium diffuses from the steel bulk to grain boundaries and the surface.
Surface-enriched chromium preferentially oxidizes to form a tightly adherent, nanostructured chromium-rich oxide film.
The chromium-rich oxide film reduces diffusion of aggressive ions such as chloride into the steel substrate.
Under irradiation, a fine-grained microstructure promotes faster repair of damaged passive-film regions by increasing chromium diffusion.
High-Cr steels with controlled grain structures and oxidation treatment will have lower corrosion current densities than lower-Cr, coarse-grained, surface-chromium-depleted, or untreated controls.
High-Cr steels with controlled grain structures and oxidation treatment will have higher pitting potentials than the controls.
Treated samples will exhibit a uniform nanoscale chromium-rich passive layer, whereas untreated controls will exhibit a disrupted or thinner oxide layer.
Lower chromium content, coarse grains, or surface chromium depletion lead to discontinuous or less protective oxide films.
Steels with discontinuous or less protective oxide films exhibit more pitting and uniform corrosion under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when steel chromium content is above approximately 12–15 wt%.
The proposed mechanism requires oxidizing conditions, moderate temperatures, and moderate corrosive-ion concentrations.
Very high chloride concentrations may cause the proposed mechanism to cease being protective.
Alternative alloying compositions that substantially alter diffusion may limit the applicability of the proposed mechanism.
The qualitative roles of chromium segregation and passive-film formation in corrosion resistance are well established.
The quantitative effects of oxide nanostructure, chromium content, grain size, and simultaneous irradiation on film stability and corrosion resistance remain uncertain.
The controlled study will vary chromium content, grain size, oxidation treatment, and irradiation while comparing corrosion and passive-film properties.
Failure to form a continuous nanocrystalline chromium-rich film, or failure to reduce corrosion relative to controls, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
